result: The authors determined the cryo-EM structure of the Frh complex at near-atomic resolution (3.9-4.0 Å by 0.5 FSC criterion, 5.5 Å by gold standard). The complex is a 1.2-MDa dodecamer with tetrahedral symmetry containing 12 copies of the FrhABG heterotrimer that unexpectedly forms a spherical protein shell with a hollow core.
status_reasoning: Claims C4, C30, C6, C7, C72-C75 collectively provide strong evidence for the structure determination. The resolution estimates are provided using multiple criteria (0.5 FSC and gold standard 0.143 FSC), the stoichiometry is determined from the reconstruction, and the unexpected spherical architecture is directly observed in the cryo-EM maps. The data quality metrics and multiple independent validation approaches support these structural conclusions.

result: Each FrhABG heterotrimer contains a complete electron transfer chain with cofactors ([NiFe] center, four Fe-S clusters, and FAD) arranged in a linear pathway with inter-cofactor distances of 4-12 Å. The cryo-EM map reveals strong electron density for the chains of metal clusters running parallel to the protein shell.
status_reasoning: Claims C3, C8, C31, C36, and C106-C112 describe the cofactor composition and arrangement with specific distance measurements from the structural model. The electron density for metal clusters is directly observed in the cryo-EM maps (C8), and the distances between cofactors (4-12 Å) are appropriate for electron transfer. The complete chain of cofactors in each heterotrimer is well-documented in the density maps.

result: The polypeptide chains of all three subunits were traced, with FrhB built de novo from the EM map as it has no structural homolog. The final model contains 878 of 903 residues with 88.1% in favored Ramachandran regions, 8.0% in allowed regions, and 3.8% outliers.
status_reasoning: Claims C5, C32, C52, C88-C93, C101, and C115-C118 document the model building process and validation. The de novo building of FrhB is supported by multiple lines of evidence including secondary structure prediction confirmation (C91), glycine residue patterns (C92), and visibility of Fe-S cluster density (C89). The Ramachandran statistics (88.1% favored) are reasonable for a 3.9-4.0 Å resolution structure, though the 3.8% outliers suggest some regions may be less well-defined.

result: FrhA shows considerable homology to group 1 [NiFe]-hydrogenase large subunits with a conserved [NiFe] center. FrhG has an N-terminal domain homologous to group 1 small subunits and a C-terminal ferredoxin domain with two [4Fe4S] clusters. A 12-residue stretch (188-199) in FrhG is disordered, and the N-terminus likely starts at Val39 rather than the genome-annotated position.
status_reasoning: Claims C37-C50 describe the structural characterization of FrhA and FrhG through homology modeling and comparison with known structures. The homology to group 1 enzymes is supported by structural fitting (C39), and the ferredoxin domain assignment is based on sequence motifs (C42) confirmed by density (C45). The missing N-terminal density (C48) and alternative start codon interpretation (C49) are reasonable given the lack of density and literature on archaeal translation initiation.

result: The F420-binding site was identified in FrhB by comparing cryo-EM maps with and without substrate. The isoalloxazine ring of F420 is positioned ~4 Å from the FAD isoalloxazine ring in a conserved pocket with easy surface access. F420 binding does not induce major conformational changes.
status_reasoning: Claims C53-C64, C68-C69, and C82-C86 provide convergent evidence for F420 binding site identification. The differential density between substrate-free and substrate-bound maps (C53, C57) consistently shows additional density at the same location across refinement stages. The proximity to FAD (C59, C85), conservation of surrounding residues (C60, C61, C86), and lack of major conformational changes (C69) all support the assignment. Conserved regions of FrhB cluster near the FAD and F420-binding site, with a poorly resolved C-terminal helix containing conserved residues near the putative F420 entrance channel.

result: The structural models show expected protein folding characteristics: hydrophobic residues form protein cores while charged residues face outward, hydrophobic pockets are present in all three subunits, and FrhB contains a buried hydrophobic helix. Only FrhG has missing internal density (residues 188-199), likely forming a flexible surface loop.

result: FrhB shows sequence homology to other F420-binding proteins, with highly conserved residues clustering around the Fe-S cluster, FAD, and F420-binding sites.

result: The Frh complex shows no preferred orientation in vitreous ice due to its spherical shape, and the complex is very rigid with no detectable conformational changes upon F420 binding at the current resolution. The tetrahedral symmetry provides 12 asymmetric units per particle.

result: Frh was purified from Methanothermobacter marburgensis under anaerobic conditions. Cryo-EM data were collected on an FEI Tecnai Polara at 200 kV on film, with final datasets containing 84,000 particles (substrate-free) and 97,000 particles (with F420). Tetrahedral symmetry was applied throughout processing with iterative refinement and particle selection.

result: Background knowledge claims establish that Frh is a group 3 [NiFe]-hydrogenase that reduces F420 in methanogenic archaea, accounting for ~1% of cytoplasmic protein. Prior negative stain EM studies interpreted the complex as a flat cylinder of 6-8 heterotrimers, and only group 1 [NiFe]-hydrogenase structures had been determined by crystallography prior to this work.
